events.title: Ghana — Post Distribution Monitoring Report: Anloga District and Keta Municipal (October 2026)
events.summary: Country: Ghana Source: International Organization for Migration Please refer to the attached file. The International Organization for Migration (IOM), in collaboration with the National Disaster Management Organization (NADMO), conducted a Post-Distribution Monitoring (PDM) exercise among households that received humanitarian assistance following the 29 June 2026 floods. A total of 134 beneficiary households were monitored to assess the effectiveness, relevance, and utilization of the support provided, as well as the extent to which it addressed the immediate needs of affected households. The Post-Distribution Monitoring gathered feedback directly from beneficiaries on their level of satisfaction with the assistance received, challenges encountered during or after the distribution process, and the overall contribution of the assistance in supporting their recovery. It also assessed the accessibility, timeliness, and appropriateness of the assistance while identifying any remaining priority needs and gaps among flood-affected households. The findings provide valuable evidence to inform future humanitarian interventions, strengthen accountability to affected populations, and improve the quality and effectiveness of disaster response efforts.

events.title: World: Speed, Scale and Disregard: How new technology and changing tactics are driving civilian harm
events.summary: Countries: World, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Iran (Islamic Republic of), Lebanon, occupied Palestinian territory, Sudan, Ukraine Source: Norwegian Refugee Council Please refer to the attached file. Authors: Jenny McAvoy I Chris Rogers I Emanuela Gillard War is changing. The risks to civilians are changing with it. From the destruction of critical civilian infrastructure to the growing use of drones and AI-assisted targeting systems, evolving patterns of warfare are exposing civilians to devastating and far-reaching harm. Drawing on research across six contexts where the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) supports people affected by displacement, this report examines how and why civilians are being harmed - and what can be done to protect them. Across the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Gaza, the Islamic Republic of Iran, Lebanon, Sudan and Ukraine, it identifies two particularly concerning trends: the widespread destruction of infrastructure, disrupting access to essential services, and the growing use of emerging military technologies, raising new challenges for civilian protection and compliance with international humanitarian law. Much of the resulting suffering is foreseeable and can be prevented or reduced. Reversing this trajectory requires action from parties to conflict and the states that support them. The report calls for greater use of political, military and economic leverage to strengthen compliance with international humanitarian law and efforts to mitigate civilian harm; improved military practices and oversight; earlier investment in restoring damaged civilian infrastructure; and better documentation and analysis of civilian harm to inform efforts to protect civilians.

events.title: Afghanistan: Enough Room to Return? Where 7.2 million Afghan returnees settled, and whether public health services, rentals, and wages can accommodate them
events.summary: Countries: Afghanistan, Iran (Islamic Republic of), Pakistan Source: Data for Afghanistan Please refer to the attached file. Author: Ahmad Zia Wahdat, PhD Between 2021 and October 2026, about 7.2 million Afghans returned from Iran, Pakistan and elsewhere, and one in seven people now living in Afghanistan is a returnee. This independent report by Data for Afghanistan places every returnee in one of Afghanistan's 401 districts. It then measures that number against the people, inhabited land, public health workers, wages, rent and prices already there. It draws only on open and publicly accessible data from IOM, UNHCR, the Ministry of Public Health, WFP and the National Statistics and Information Authority. It introduces a district typology that separates two kinds of pressure: the returnee share of residents and spatial crowding (returnees per km² of inhabited land). The report also includes a stress test for a further one million returnees, recommendations for organizations, and profiles of all 34 provinces with district-level tables. Return is highly concentrated. Ten districts hold 21% of all returnees, and in Kunduz, Daykundi and Herat close to one resident in four is a returnee. In "saturated" districts, both the returnee share and crowding are above the national average, and 45% of returnees live in these districts. Nationally, there are 252 returnees for every public health worker, and more than 550 in Takhar and Kunduz. Yet new public health facilities over the past five years mostly opened elsewhere. In no province can one unskilled wage keep a returnee household of 6.1 members above the poverty line: it covers only 37% to 76%.
